thermal_stratification_intensification->: A stable layer of warm surface water mixes less with deeper water. This limits the movement of absorbed carbon away from the surface and can reduce how effectively the ocean takes up more.
crop_yield_volatility->food_insecurity: Unreliable harvests can reduce local food supplies and increase prices. Households may then find it harder to obtain enough nutritious food.
food_import_exposure->food_insecurity: Reliance on imported food exposes households to supply and price changes elsewhere. Disruptions can make enough nutritious food harder to afford or obtain.
food_insecurity->migration: Long-lasting difficulty obtaining enough food can push people to leave their homes. Jobs, conflict and other economic conditions also influence whether people move.
fertilizer_production->nutrient_pollutio: Making and using fertilisers increases the amount of nitrogen and phosphorus available in the environment. Some can escape into rivers and coastal waters if losses are not controlled.
nitrogen_fertilizer_runoff->nutrient_pol: Nitrogen that crops do not absorb can wash or drain into waterways. It can encourage excessive algae growth and the oxygen loss that follows.
wastewater_bypass_discharge->nutrient_po: Sewage released without adequate treatment carries nitrogen and phosphorus into water. These nutrients can worsen pollution in rivers, lakes and coastal areas.
nutrient_pollution->harmful_algal_blooms: Extra nutrients can help harmful algae grow rapidly. Light, water movement and temperature also determine whether a harmful bloom develops.
marine_heatwaves->seagrass_meadow_declin: Unusually hot seawater can damage seagrass and kill plants. Severe or repeated events can reduce the area and condition of these underwater meadows.
estuary_eutrophication->seagrass_meadow_: Excess nutrients encourage algae to grow in the water and on seagrass leaves. This can block the light that seagrass needs to survive.
coastal_erosion->seagrass_meadow_decline: Erosion and shifting sediment can wash away or bury seagrass habitat. Meadows may shrink where roots cannot remain established.
urban_tree_canopy_loss->urban_heat_islan: Losing city trees removes shade and cooling from water released by leaves. Nearby streets, buildings and air can become hotter.
urban_sprawl_housing->urban_heat_island: Outward housing growth can replace vegetation with roofs, roads and other surfaces that store heat. This can increase local warming within built-up areas.
asphalt_pavement_heat_absorbers->urban_h: Dark asphalt absorbs sunlight during the day and releases stored heat later. Large paved areas can keep nearby places warmer after sunset.
urban_heat_island->public_health_heat_bu: Extra daytime and nighttime heat in cities increases people's exposure to high temperatures. This can add to illness risks, especially where cooling is limited.
snowmelt_timing_shift->peak_glacier_runo: Earlier snowmelt changes the seasonal mix of snow and glacier water reaching rivers. It can make the loss of late-season glacier support more noticeable, without alone proving that a basin has passed its maximum glacier runoff.
snow_drought->peak_glacier_runoff_passag: Less stored winter snow can make a river basin more dependent on glacier melt. Once that glacier contribution begins declining, late-season water supplies become more exposed.
peak_glacier_runoff_passage->glacier_mel: After a glacier basin passes its period of greatest meltwater supply, the contribution can decline over time. People and power systems relying on that water may face less dependable dry-season flows.
temp->marine_pathogen_range_expansion: Warming coastal water can make more places or longer seasons suitable for temperature-sensitive germs such as Vibrio bacteria. This can affect seafood safety and exposure through contact with water.
coastal_inundation_risk->marine_pathogen: Rising seawater can change salt levels in estuaries. This may make particular places more or less suitable for disease-causing organisms, depending on the salt range they tolerate.
marine_pathogen_range_expansion->public_: Some marine germs can cause illness through seafood or contact with open wounds. Their spread can add pressure to coastal health services. This is an infection pathway, rather than heat injury itself.
sea_ice_season_loss->coastal_permafrost_: A longer open-water season gives waves more time and space to attack Arctic coasts. Shores made of thawing, ice-rich ground can erode especially quickly.
temp->coastal_permafrost_erosion: Warmer air and sea water thaw ice-rich coastal ground and make it easier for waves to wear away. The effect is strongest along exposed, vulnerable shorelines.
coastal_permafrost_erosion->polar_infras: Rapid erosion and collapsing coastal slopes can remove support beneath buildings, roads and pipes. Communities may lose reliable access and essential services.
ocean_heat_content->antarctic_shelf_inst: Warmer water beneath Antarctic ice shelves melts them from below. Thinner shelves provide less support to the land ice behind them.
temp->antarctic_shelf_instability: Warming can destabilise Antarctic ice shelves through warmer surrounding seas. In some places, surface meltwater can also widen cracks and contribute to break-up.
antarctic_shelf_instability->sea_level_r: Floating shelves help hold back ice on land. When they weaken, inland ice can flow into the ocean faster and add to sea-level rise.
marine_heatwaves->shell_calcification_fa: Unusually hot seawater can make it harder for young shellfish to grow and form shells. This may add to stress from changing water chemistry, with different limits for each species.
estuary_eutrophication->shell_calcificat: Excess nutrients can encourage growth and decay that use oxygen and release carbon dioxide into coastal water. The resulting conditions can make shell formation harder for vulnerable animals.
shell_calcification_failures->marine_foo: When shellfish and shell-forming plankton grow less well or die, animals feeding on them may lose food. Habitats and food chains can change where these species play an important role.
sea_ice_season_loss->ice_albedo_feedback: Losing sea ice during the sunlit season exposes darker ocean water. The water absorbs more sunlight, adding heat that can encourage further melting.
cryoconite_hole_expansion->ice_albedo_fe: Dark sediment and living material on snow or ice can reduce the sunlight reflected away. Exposed dark patches may then melt more quickly.
ice_albedo_feedback_loops->arctic_amplif: As reflective snow and ice disappear, the Arctic absorbs more sunlight. This is one of the processes that helps the region warm faster than the global average.
particulate_soot_levels->black_carbon_de: More soot in the air provides more material that can settle onto snow and ice. Rain, snow and air movement affect where it is deposited.
wildfire_regime_shift->black_carbon_depo: Large or severe fires can release soot that travels downwind. Some may settle on snow and ice, depending on transport and weather conditions.
shipping->black_carbon_deposition: Ship engines can release soot when they burn fuel. Winds may carry some of it to snow and ice, especially in nearby regions.
crop_yield_volatility->staple_food_price: Poor harvests of major food crops can tighten supplies and make prices less stable. Stored reserves and substitute foods can soften the effect.
fertilizer_price_shock->staple_food_pric: Higher fertiliser prices raise farming costs and may lead to lower use. Smaller later harvests can add pressure to prices of basic foods.
shipping_lane_disruption->staple_food_pr: Disrupted sea routes can delay food and farming supplies or make delivery more expensive. These changes can increase swings in market prices.
staple_food_price_volatility->food_insec: Sharp or unpredictable changes in basic food prices make household budgets harder to manage. Families with little income or stored food can struggle to buy enough.
irrigation_water_inefficiency->topsoil_s: Poorly managed irrigation and drainage can leave dissolved salts around plant roots. Salty groundwater rising toward the surface can add to the build-up.
groundwater_depletion->topsoil_salinizat: Falling groundwater supplies can force use of poorer-quality water or change how salty water moves. Soil salt levels can rise where irrigation and drainage allow salts to collect.
coastal_inundation_risk->topsoil_saliniz: Seawater entering fields or freshwater supplies brings dissolved salts with it. Salt left around crop roots can make farming more difficult on low-lying land.
arctic_amplification_rates->jet_stream_v: Faster Arctic warming can reduce the temperature contrast with lower latitudes near the surface. This may favour some weaker or more winding jet-stream patterns in certain seasons, but it does not determine their behaviour.
pacific_decadal_oscillation->jet_stream_: Long-lasting North Pacific sea-temperature patterns can influence winds high in the atmosphere. This can affect the jet stream over the Pacific and North America, alongside its own natural variability.
jet_stream_volatility->blocking_pattern_: A slow or strongly winding jet stream can help weather patterns remain in place. Other atmospheric conditions still determine whether a long-lasting block develops.
dam_and_diversion_infrastructure->riveri: Dams and water diversions can block movement and separate river habitats. Their effects need evidence about the actual barriers and the species trying to pass them.
road_stream_crossing_barriers->riverine_: Poorly designed pipes, crossings and gates can stop aquatic animals moving along streams. Whether a crossing acts as a barrier depends on its design and the species involved.
levee_and_channelization_works->riverine: Embankments and straightened channels can cut rivers off from nearby floodplains and side habitats. Documented barriers are needed to assess how much wildlife movement is restricted.
dam_and_diversion_infrastructure->river_: Storing or diverting river water changes when and how much water reaches places downstream. Operating rules can reduce seasonal peaks or create new daily fluctuations.
dam_and_diversion_infrastructure->coasta: Dams can trap sediment that would otherwise reach a river delta or beach. Waves and currents may then remove coastal material faster than it is replaced.
road_stream_crossing_barriers->river_flo: Narrow or poorly placed stream crossings can change water speed, depth and sediment movement nearby. These are local effects that need comparison with an unobstructed stretch of stream.
road_stream_crossing_barriers->freshwate: Barriers at stream crossings can stop animals reaching shelter or breeding areas. Repeated isolation can reduce populations and make recovery after damage harder.
levee_and_channelization_works->river_fl: Straightening or confining rivers can move water downstream faster and separate it from floodplain storage. This changes local depths, speeds and flooding patterns.
levee_and_channelization_works->freshwat: Removing side channels and floodplain connections reduces the variety of river habitats. Fish and other wildlife may lose places to feed, breed or shelter.
humanitarian_response_funding_shortfall-: Insufficient funding can force aid organisations to delay, reduce or close programmes. The effect depends on each operation's needs, access and freedom to use the funds.
humanitarian_access_constraints->humanit: Conflict, restrictions and attacks can stop aid workers reaching people. Supplies and funding cannot meet needs if access remains blocked.
humanitarian_surge_demand->humanitarian_: Several disasters or conflicts occurring together can create more needs than aid services can meet. The shortfall depends on the capacity and circumstances of each response.
agricultural_groundwater_withdrawal->gro: Pumping groundwater for irrigation lowers reserves when withdrawals keep exceeding replacement. A record of water use alone does not show that an underground store is shrinking.
municipal_groundwater_withdrawal->ground: Pumping groundwater for public supplies can lower water levels if use stays above replacement. Other sources or reduced demand can change that balance.
industrial_groundwater_withdrawal->groun: Factories, mines and power facilities can reduce groundwater reserves when sustained pumping exceeds replacement. The actual balance must be assessed for the underground water body concerned.
agricultural_nitrogen_application->nitro: Microbes can turn some nitrogen added to farm soil into nitrous oxide, a heat-trapping gas. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change's basic method estimates 0.010 kilograms of nitrogen released in this gas per kilogram of qualifying nitrogen added, with a default uncertainty range of 0.002–0.018.
nitrogen_fertilizer_runoff->nitrous_oxid: Nitrogen washed from fields can be changed by microbes in downstream soils and water. Some is released as nitrous oxide, adding an indirect source of emissions.
industry_farming->nitrous_oxide: Manure, crop remains and other nitrogen inputs can release nitrous oxide through soil processes. Emissions depend on the practices and conditions. The basic Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change estimate for qualifying managed-soil inputs is 1% of added nitrogen, with a default range of 0.2–1.8%.
fertilizer_production->nitrous_oxide: Making nitric acid for some fertilisers produces nitrous oxide as a by-product. This link applies to that manufacturing process, not to every type of fertiliser production.
nitrous_oxide->temp: Nitrous oxide traps heat and remains in the air for a long time. Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change estimates its past emissions contributed about 0.09°C of warming in 2010–2019 compared with 1850–1900, with a very likely range of about 0.05–0.16°C.
coal_power_sulfur_emissions->sulfur_diox: Sulfur in coal forms sulfur dioxide when the fuel burns. The amount released depends on the fuel and how effectively the plant cleans its exhaust.
shipping->sulfur_dioxide: Sulfur in ship fuel can form sulfur dioxide during burning. Fuel standards and exhaust-cleaning equipment determine how much escapes.
steel->sulfur_dioxide: Sulfur in steelmaking fuels and raw materials can be released as sulfur dioxide. Capture and treatment equipment affect the final amount emitted.
sulfur_dioxide->acid_rain_deposition: Sulfur dioxide reacts in the air to form sulfuric acid. It can then reach the ground in rain, snow or dry particles, sometimes far from its source.
sulfur_dioxide->pm2_5_particulates: Some sulfur dioxide changes into tiny sulfate-containing particles in the air. These become part of fine-particle pollution.
road_freight_diesel_lock_in->carbon_mono: Diesel trucks can release carbon monoxide when fuel does not burn completely. Engine condition, controls and operating load affect how much is produced.
shipping->carbon_monoxide: Ship engines can produce carbon monoxide when fuel burns incompletely. A useful estimate needs details about the engine, fuel and how the vessel operates.
wildfire_regime_shift->carbon_monoxide: Wildfires produce carbon monoxide as material burns incompletely. The amount varies with the fuel and burning conditions.
carbon_monoxide->air_pollution_health_bu: Breathing carbon monoxide reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen. Risk depends on the amount breathed, exposure time and the person's condition. Detecting the gas alone does not measure health harm.
industry_farming->rice_paddy_methane_bub: Flooded rice fields create soil conditions with little oxygen. Decaying organic material can then produce methane.
food->rice_paddy_methane_bubbles: Demand for rice can increase the area or intensity of flooded cultivation. The response also depends on yields, trade, diets and available water.
extreme_precipitation_intensity->combine: Heavy rain can send more runoff into pipes that carry both rainwater and sewage. Overflow occurs only where such a combined system exists and the incoming water exceeds its capacity.
urbanization->combined_sewer_overflow: Hard urban surfaces can send rainwater quickly into combined rainwater and sewage pipes. Overflow risk rises where storage and pipe capacity cannot handle the flow.
marine_heatwaves->coral_bleaching: Prolonged unusually warm seawater can disrupt the partnership between corals and the tiny algae living inside them. Corals may turn pale, with responses differing between species and reefs.
ocean_acidification->coral_bleaching: Changing seawater chemistry can reduce coral growth and recovery. It can make heat stress harder to withstand, but it is not itself a measure of heat-related bleaching.
nutrient_pollution->coral_bleaching: Excess nutrients and organic matter can add stress to coastal reefs. This may make heat-related bleaching and recovery worse, depending on local conditions.
snow_drought->alpine_snowpack_declines: A season with little snowfall or unusually early melting leaves less water stored in mountain snow. The change differs with elevation, season and river basin.
soot_deposition_on_snow->alpine_snowpack: Soot darkens snow so it absorbs more sunlight. Enough soot and sunshine can speed melting, with effects varying between mountain areas and seasons.
cattle_stocking_density->cattle_grazing_: More cattle on the same land create more hoof pressure. Soil can become tightly packed where wetness, soil type and limited recovery make it vulnerable.
coal_power_sulfur_emissions->acid_rain_d: Coal-burning releases sulfur dioxide, which can turn into acid and settle downwind. Emissions at a power station do not by themselves show how much reaches a particular place.
agricultural_soil_compaction->soil_micro: Tightly packed farm soil restricts the movement of air and water. This can make conditions less suitable for some of the microbes that support healthy soil.
urban_hydrologic_supply_shortfall->urban: When water supplies fall short of demand, utilities may limit use to protect essential needs. Restrictions are an operating decision, not an automatic result of a dry period.
urban_water_demand_peak->urban_water_rat: High demand can use up the spare capacity in a city's water supply. Utilities may impose restrictions, especially during drought, depending on their operating choices.
urban_distribution_water_loss->urban_wat: Leaks and other physical losses reduce the water that reaches customers. When supply is tight, this can contribute to stronger restrictions on use.
urban_source_water_treatment_constraint-: Poor source-water quality can reduce how much a treatment plant can safely supply. Utilities may restrict use while dealing with the problem, but the decision depends on local conditions.
wildfire_smoke_pm25_exposure->wildfire_s: Fine particles in wildfire smoke can worsen heart and lung illness and increase hospital visits. Actual admissions depend on exposure and the population affected, not just the presence of smoke.
wildfire_smoke_exposure_duration->wildfi: Longer or repeated smoke exposure gives more time for harmful effects on the heart and lungs. Hospital admissions still need to be measured rather than assumed from the smoke alone.
surface_water_inflow_deficit->surface_wa: Less rain, runoff or river inflow means less water entering lakes, wetlands and reservoirs. Storage can fall if other inflows do not make up the loss.
surface_water_evaporative_loss->surface_: Evaporation removes water from lakes and reservoirs. Their levels can fall when incoming water does not replace it.
surface_water_groundwater_exchange_shift: Some lakes and wetlands exchange water with underground reserves. Changes in that exchange can raise or lower the amount stored at the surface.
surface_water_withdrawal_pressure->surfa: Taking or diverting water can reduce lake and reservoir storage. The effect depends on how withdrawals compare with incoming water and operating rules.
temp->freeze_thaw_rock_fracturing: Repeated changes around freezing can make water in existing rock cracks freeze and thaw. The resulting pressure can gradually loosen or move pieces of rock.
extreme_precipitation_intensity->freeze_: Heavy rain or rapid snowmelt can fill cracks in rock. Later freezing and thawing, together with water pressure, can weaken blocks that are already vulnerable.
permafrost_thaw->freeze_thaw_rock_fractu: Ice in rock cracks can help hold pieces in place. When it thaws, the rock loses support and becomes more exposed to seasonal water and temperature changes.
ice_sheet_mass_loss->fjord_sedimentation: Thinning and retreating ice can expose sediment and change meltwater routes. This changes when and how much material reaches nearby coastal inlets.
peak_glacier_runoff_passage->fjord_sedim: Meltwater carries fine rock and soil into the water below glaciers. How much arrives, and at what depth, depends on the amount of water and how it enters the basin.
extreme_precipitation_intensity->fjord_s: Heavy rain can wash loose material from glacier-fed rivers and deltas. Short bursts of flow may carry fine particles and larger sediment into nearby coastal waters.
glacier_calving_events->fjord_sedimentat: Breaking ice and falling icebergs can disturb sediment near a glacier front. Underwater slides and cloudy currents may move material that had already settled.
shipping->inland_waterway_fuel_spills: Collisions, running aground and fuel transfers can damage a vessel or its fuel lines. Spilled fuel can then enter a river, canal or nearby shore.
critical_infrastructure_fragility->inlan: Failure of a fuel tank, pipe, hose or protective barrier can allow fuel to reach nearby water. The risk depends on the damaged equipment and its connection to the waterway.
extreme_precipitation_intensity->inland_: Floods can expose or damage fuel pipes and overwhelm barriers around storage. High flows can also carry an existing spill into a river more quickly.
coastal_groundwater_withdrawal->coastal_: Heavy pumping near a coast can reduce the freshwater flowing toward the sea. Saltwater may then move into areas that previously held fresh groundwater.

carbon_emission->extreme_precipitation_i: Carbon dioxide adds to warming, allowing the air to hold more water vapour. Storms can produce heavier rain when enough moisture and rising air are available.
carbon_emission->tropical_cyclone_rapid_: Carbon dioxide adds heat to the air and ocean. Warmer upper-ocean water can help cyclones strengthen rapidly when winds, humidity and other storm conditions are also favourable.
carbon_emission->water_stress: Warming caused by carbon dioxide changes evaporation and water supplies. This can worsen shortages where demand is already high compared with the water available.
carbon_emission->heat_related_mortality_: Carbon dioxide adds to warming and more dangerous heat. Greater exposure can increase heat-related death risks, especially where people lack cooling and health care.
carbon_emission->occupational_heat_expos: Warming makes strenuous work outdoors or in uncooled buildings more difficult and dangerous. Workers may need more rest and shorter exposure to avoid heat illness.
carbon_emission->snowmelt_timing_shift: Warming can turn more winter precipitation into rain and bring earlier snowmelt. The timing change depends on the river basin, elevation and season.
carbon_emission->soil_moisture_collapse: Warming increases evaporation and the water needs of plants. Soil can dry sharply when rain and irrigation do not replace the loss.
carbon_emission->flash_flood_regime: Warming can intensify short bursts of heavy rain. Sudden flood risk also depends on slopes, soil, drains and what lies in the path of the water.
carbon_emission->drought_persistence: Warming increases the air's demand for moisture. Where rain stays low, soil and plants can dry faster and drought conditions may last longer.
carbon_emission->freshwater_lens_compres: Warming contributes to rising seas and coastal flooding. On low islands, salty water can then reduce the shallow underground layer of fresh water people rely on.
carbon_emission->glacial_lake_failure_ri: Warming makes glaciers retreat and changes lakes of meltwater around them. Flood danger increases where unstable barriers hold back water above exposed communities.
carbon_emission->sea_ice_season_loss: The cited study found that Arctic September sea-ice area fell roughly in step with accumulated human carbon dioxide emissions. Over its assessed record, each extra metric tonne was associated with about 3 square metres less ice, with an uncertainty of plus or minus 0.3 square metres.
carbon_emission->polar_infrastructure_fa: Warming contributes to thawing frozen ground and losing protective sea ice. These changes can damage buildings, roads and services in polar regions.
carbon_emission->snow_drought: Warming can shift snowfall toward rain and speed melting. Mountain areas may then store much less water in winter snow than expected.
carbon_emission->glacier_meltwater_depen: Warming changes glacier size and when meltwater reaches rivers. People, farms and power systems that depend on that water can face less reliable supplies.
carbon_emission->oceanic_deoxygenation: Warming makes seawater hold less oxygen and can reduce mixing between surface and deep water. These processes contribute to declining oxygen in parts of the ocean.
carbon_emission->antarctic_bottom_water_: Warming and additional meltwater change water conditions around Antarctica. Lighter surface water may sink less readily, weakening the formation of dense water that spreads along the deep ocean floor.
carbon_emission->marine_fisheries_collap: Under the high-emissions pathway RCP8.5, Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change projects global maximum fish catch potential to fall by 20.5–24.1% in 2081–2100 compared with 1986–2005. This is a scenario-based estimate of potential catch, not a prediction that every fishery will change by the same amount.
carbon_emission->ocean_current_regime_sh: Warming changes the heat and freshwater entering the ocean. These changes can alter currents, with different responses in different ocean regions.
carbon_emission->coastal_hypoxia: Warming can reduce oxygen in coastal water and limit mixing with deeper layers. In nutrient-rich areas, faster decay and weaker mixing can worsen oxygen shortages.
carbon_emission->marine_food_web_simplif: Carbon dioxide changes ocean temperature and chemistry, with further effects on oxygen and currents. Some species lose suitable conditions or food, and repeated losses can leave a less varied food web.
carbon_emission->ocean_salinity_stratifi: Warming changes rain, evaporation and ice melt. In some ocean regions, the resulting differences in salt content and temperature strengthen the separation between surface and deeper water.
carbon_emission->littoral_surge_vulnerab: Warming expands seawater and melts ice on land, raising the starting level of the sea. Storm-driven water can then reach farther inland along low coasts.
carbon_emission->ocean_carbon_uptake_wea: Warming can make ocean layers mix less and slow the movement of carbon into deep water. This can weaken ocean uptake compared with what would happen without that climate change.
carbon_emission->ocean_heat_content: Carbon dioxide reduces how easily Earth loses heat to space. The ocean takes up most of the extra heat, storing it from the surface into deeper water.
carbon_emission->nocturnal_heat_stress: Warming raises nighttime temperatures and can reduce relief after hot days. Repeated hot nights give the body less chance to cool and recover.
carbon_emission->compound_day_night_heat: Warming raises both daytime highs and nighttime lows. Long runs of weather that limit cooling can then produce consecutive hot days and nights.
carbon_emission->lightning_fire_weather: Warming can dry vegetation and create hotter fire-prone conditions. Lightning can start fires when thunderstorms bring too little rain to wet that dry material.
carbon_emission->biodiversity_intactness: Warming shifts the conditions that plants and animals can tolerate and the places where they can survive. These pressures add to habitat loss, harvesting and other human activities.
carbon_emission->wildfire_regime_shift: Warming can increase heat and drying, changing when and how intensely fires burn. Fires still need burnable material and a source of ignition.
carbon_emission->freshwater_ecosystem_co: Warming changes water temperatures, river flow and flood or drought extremes. These changes can put freshwater plants and animals under pressure.
carbon_emission->crop_yield_volatility: Heat, drought and heavy rain can affect flowering, seed growth and harvest timing. Different exposure between seasons and regions can make crop harvests less dependable.
carbon_emission->farm_heat_stress: Warmer growing seasons can strain crops, livestock and farm workers. Reproduction, safe working time and farm output may all be affected.
carbon_emission->livestock_disease_press: Warming changes heat stress and conditions for some disease-carrying insects. Livestock disease also depends on animal care, movement and trade.
carbon_emission->food_insecurity: Warming-related heat, drought and floods can damage harvests and food transport. Higher prices or reduced supplies make adequate food harder to obtain for households with little money or reserves.
carbon_emission->migration: Climate hazards can repeatedly damage homes, water supplies and livelihoods. Some people may move temporarily or permanently when they cannot recover safely where they live.
carbon_emission->public_health_heat_burd: More frequent or severe heat increases exposure to conditions that can cause illness. Health services and people without reliable cooling can face greater pressure.
carbon_emission->vector_borne_disease_ex: Changes in temperature and rain can make some places suitable for disease-carrying insects for longer. Effects vary by disease and can reverse where conditions become too hot or dry.
carbon_emission->critical_infrastructure: Heat, floods, fires and coastal hazards can damage power, water, transport and communications equipment. Repeated damage can shorten its useful life and interrupt connected services.
carbon_emission->marine_heatwaves: Under the very high-emissions scenario SSP5-8.5, marine heatwaves are projected to occur eight times as often globally in 2081–2100 as in 1995–2014. The assessed likely range is three to fifteen times. This is a scenario estimate, not a guaranteed outcome.
carbon_emission->coral_bleaching: Warmer seawater can disrupt the tiny algae that live inside corals and provide much of their food. Corals may turn pale, and prolonged stress can kill colonies.
carbon_emission->sea_level_rise: Warming makes seawater expand and melts ice stored on land. Both processes raise average sea level.
carbon_emission->floodplain_exposure: Heavier rain can increase flood hazards. Risk rises where homes, people and important services occupy land that rivers can flood.
carbon_emission->waterborne_pathogen_out: Warming and heavy rain can favour some germs, overwhelm sanitation and wash pollution into water. Disease outbreaks depend on whether treatment and public-health systems contain the exposure.
subsea_cables->telecom_backbone: Undersea fibre cables carry information between coastal landing stations and land-based networks. They provide important international connections for calls, data and online services.
subsea_cables->ai_data_centers: Fast international cable links help move data and deliver computing services between facilities. Data-centre growth also depends on electricity, chips, land-based networks and customer demand.
subsea_cables->critical_infrastructure_f: Damage to an undersea cable can interrupt services that depend on it. The disruption is greater where there are few alternative routes, landing points or spare connections.
food->palm_oil_canopy_clearance: Demand for palm-containing products can encourage more production. Forest loss occurs only when the extra supply comes from clearing forest, rather than higher yields or land that was already cleared. This differs greatly between regions.
industry_farming->palm_oil_canopy_cleara: Establishing an oil-palm plantation can remove forest if it expands onto forested land. A plantation's presence alone does not prove recent clearing. Earlier land cover and timing need to be checked.
personal_conveyance->palm_oil_canopy_cle: Road-fuel demand can add pressure for palm-oil production where fuel contains palm-based biodiesel. Forest impacts depend on where extra supply comes from, yields and land protection. The link does not apply where palm oil is not used in transport fuel.
palm_oil_canopy_clearance->biodiversity_: Replacing tropical forest with oil palms removes and separates habitats used by forest species. Keeping forest patches and improving plantation management can help, but does not recreate the original forest community.
wetlands_drainage_scales->peatland_degra: Draining peatland exposes wet organic soil to air. The soil can decay, sink and lose the water conditions and plants that support a healthy wetland.
deforestation->peatland_degradations: Clearing plants from peatland often comes with drainage or conversion to another use. This can expose stored peat and remove plants that help build and protect it.
wildfire_regime_shift->peatland_degradat: Severe or repeated fires can burn peat, kill plants and change how water moves through the land. Recovery can become more difficult after repeated damage.
peatland_degradations->peat_oxidation_pu: Damaged peatland can lose the high water table that keeps buried plant material wet. Exposure to air allows faster decay and greater carbon loss.
wetlands_drainage_scales->wetland_peat_f: Draining peat lowers its moisture and makes it easier to ignite. Once burning, dry peat can smoulder for a long time below the surface.
wildfire_regime_shift->wetland_peat_fire: Longer or more severe fire seasons increase the chance that fire reaches dry peat. Repeated burning can occur before the wetland has recovered.
peatland_degradations->wetland_peat_fire: Damage to wetland plants and water flow can leave peat dry and exposed. Fires may start more easily, burn deeper and become harder to put out.
wetland_peat_fires->carbon_emission: Burning peat releases carbon stored over long periods as carbon dioxide and other pollutants. The amount depends partly on the area burned and how deep the fire reaches.
wet_bulb_heat->cooling_equity_gaps: Dangerous hot and humid conditions increase the need for effective cooling. People who cannot afford or reach safe indoor spaces face a wider protection gap.
energy_affordability_crisis->cooling_equ: High energy costs can stop households from buying or running enough cooling. Having an electricity connection or an air conditioner does not ensure that using it is affordable.
utility_disconnection_risk->cooling_equi: An electricity shutoff stops powered cooling when people may need it most. Households with health conditions can be especially vulnerable during dangerous heat.
adaptation_capital_shortfall->cooling_eq: Too little investment can delay cooler housing, shaded spaces and public cooling facilities. Communities already receiving fewer services may remain less protected.
cooling_equity_gaps->public_health_heat_: People unable to keep indoor temperatures safe face greater heat illness risks. Older people, those with existing illness and households with limited resources may be especially exposed.
marine_heatwaves->coral_larval_mortality: Seawater above the temperatures young corals can tolerate can reduce survival and successful settlement. Effects vary by species and stage of growth.
coral_bleaching->coral_larval_mortality: Stressed adult corals may have less energy to reproduce and support their young. Fewer larvae may be produced, or fewer may survive and settle successfully.
ocean_acidification->coral_larval_mortal: Changing seawater chemistry can interfere with early coral growth and the signals young corals use to find a place to settle. Sensitive species may have lower survival.
coral_larval_mortality->reef_structural_: If too few young corals survive and establish themselves, they cannot replace lost adults. Over time this can weaken the living cover and solid structure of a reef.
temp->tropospheric_ozone: Hot, sunny weather with little air movement can help ground-level ozone build up. The gases that form it, clouds and air mixing also matter, so temperature alone does not determine pollution.
tropospheric_ozone->air_pollution_health: Breathing ground-level ozone irritates and damages airways, especially in exposed or vulnerable people. Studies reviewed for World Health Organization guidelines also link short-term outdoor increases with a small rise in daily deaths from all causes.
tropical_cyclone_rapid_intensification->: Powerful cyclone waves and currents can break or overturn corals and move reef rubble. Damage depends on the storm's path and the reef exposed to it.
coral_bleaching->coral_reef_fragmentatio: Repeated severe heat stress can kill or weaken corals. Their remaining structures may then break or erode more easily during later disturbances.
ocean_acidification->coral_reef_fragment: Changes in seawater chemistry can slow reef building and increase erosion. Weaker structures can become more vulnerable when waves or other disturbances strike.
shipping->coral_reef_fragmentation: Ships running aground or dropping anchors can crush, break or bury corals. The damage is concentrated around the incident and any removal work.
coral_reef_fragmentation->reef_structura: Repeated breakage can remove the connected, three-dimensional structure of a reef. If growth and repair cannot keep up, habitat complexity and resistance to waves decline.
peak_glacier_runoff_passage->glacial_sil: Strong seasonal meltwater flows carry fine rock particles from glaciers. The amount and timing of sediment depend on the flow, rather than simply on whether a basin has passed its maximum glacier runoff.
glacier_hydrologic_system_floods->glacia: Sudden releases of glacier water can sweep up sediment from beneath the ice and river banks. Short bursts may carry far more material than normal seasonal flows.
extreme_precipitation_intensity->glacial: Heavy rain can wash recently exposed sediment and river-bank material into glacier-fed streams. It can add to the sediment already carried by meltwater.
glacial_siltation_streams->reservoir_sto: Sediment carried into a reservoir settles as the water slows. Continued build-up takes up storage space and can interfere with water intakes.
seagrass_meadow_decline->blue_carbon_hab: Losing seagrass removes plants that take up carbon and can expose carbon-rich seabed to erosion and decay. Stored carbon may then be lost.
mangrove_buffer_loss->blue_carbon_habita: Clearing or eroding mangroves removes trees and can disturb deep organic soils. Both hold carbon that may no longer remain stored after the damage.
wetlands_drainage_scales->blue_carbon_ha: Draining coastal wetlands removes wet conditions that protect plants and organic soils. Stored carbon becomes more exposed to decay and erosion.
blue_carbon_habitat_loss->carbon_emissio: Damage to coastal habitats can release stored carbon and reduce future uptake. Carbon actually released must be counted separately from carbon that is no longer being absorbed.
ocean_heat_content->glacier_calving_even: Warm water reaching a glacier's ocean-facing edge can melt and undercut it. The weakened front may crack and release icebergs.
temp->glacier_calving_events: Warmer air creates more meltwater on ice surfaces. Water entering cracks can deepen them and destabilise ice that is already vulnerable.
ice_shelf_grounding_line_retreat->glacie: When a glacier's grounded edge retreats into deeper water, it can lose support from the seabed. A taller, less stable ice front may then become more prone to cracking and iceberg release.
glacier_calving_events->sea_level_rise: Ice moving from land into the ocean adds water mass and raises sea level. The loss of already-floating ice matters mainly when it lets ice on land flow faster.
plastics_petrochemicals->volatile_organi: Making and handling petrochemical products can release gases from processing, storage and evaporation. The type and amount depend on the product and pollution controls.
volatile_organic_compounds->ozone_format: Some organic gases react with nitrogen oxides in sunlight to form ground-level ozone. The response depends on the mix of gases and local atmospheric conditions.
road_freight_diesel_lock_in->ozone_forma: Diesel freight releases gases that can form ground-level ozone in sunlight. Pollution may develop along transport routes or farther downwind.
urban_heat_island->nighttime_heat_retent: Dense buildings and paved surfaces store daytime heat and release it slowly after sunset. Limited vegetation also reduces cooling from evaporation.
temp->transformer_heat_failure_risk: Hot air makes it harder for an electrical transformer to release the heat it produces. Its hottest parts can become hotter still, ageing insulation faster and increasing failure risk.
grid_peak_load_stress->transformer_heat_: Carrying more electricity creates more heat inside a transformer. High demand combined with hot weather can shorten insulation life and increase the chance of failure.
transformer_heat_failure_risk->critical_: A failed transformer can interrupt electricity to essential services. Replacements can take a long time, leaving connected facilities more vulnerable until supply is restored.
nutrient_pollution->shelf_sea_hypoxia: Extra nutrients can produce more algae in shallow seas. As this material decays, it can use oxygen faster than fresh water movement replaces it near the seabed.
oceanic_deoxygenation->shelf_sea_hypoxia: Water arriving with less oxygen gives a shallow sea less protection against further oxygen loss. A smaller additional loss may then be enough to harm local marine life.
shelf_sea_hypoxia->marine_food_web_simpl: Long periods of low oxygen can kill sensitive seabed animals and push fish elsewhere. Species that tolerate these conditions may become more common, changing the food web.
cloud_albedo_shift->temp: Cloud changes affect both sunlight reflected away and heat kept near Earth. The combined effect can warm or cool the planet, so the direction must be checked rather than assumed.
nitrogen_fertilizer_runoff->estuary_eutr: Nutrients washed from fields can travel through rivers into estuaries. They can feed extra algae growth and the oxygen-consuming decay that follows.
wastewater_bypass_discharge->estuary_eut: Untreated or partly treated sewage adds nutrients and organic material to receiving water. This can encourage growth and decay that use up oxygen.
hydrological_runoff_surges->estuary_eutr: Large runoff events can quickly carry nutrients from land into an estuary. The effect depends on nutrients being present in the upstream area.
shipping->invasive_species_encroachment: Ships can carry organisms in stored water, on their hulls or with cargo. An introduced species becomes invasive only if it establishes, spreads and causes harm. Transport or detection alone does not prove that.
aviation->invasive_species_encroachment: Aircraft and cargo can move living organisms to places they would not normally reach. Most do not establish harmful populations, so flight numbers cannot be treated as a count of invasions.
temp->invasive_species_encroachment: Warming can make new places suitable for some introduced species or help them survive longer seasons. It can also make conditions worse for other invaders, so effects differ by species and region.
invasive_species_encroachment->biodivers: Harmful introduced species can displace native wildlife and change habitats or food webs. Being non-native alone does not establish harm. The effects need evidence for the species and place concerned.
marine_heatwaves->kelp_forest_collapse: Long periods of unusually warm sea water can harm kelp and reduce supplies of cool, nutrient-rich water. Brief events do not always cause lasting loss, and some forests recover when other pressures are limited.
el_nino->kelp_forest_collapse: Some warm Pacific events bring both warmer coastal water and powerful waves that damage kelp. Effects vary greatly by location, and nearby forests can respond differently to the same event.
wastewater_bypass_discharge->kelp_forest: Sewage pollution can harm kelp growth and reproduction where contaminated water reaches the habitat. Lasting loss requires evidence of the exposure, its duration and the plants' response.
kelp_forest_collapse->marine_food_web_si: Losing kelp removes food and complex shelter used by many marine animals. The food web may change, but temporary loss can recover before lasting changes occur.
drought_persistence->aquifer_recharge_fa: Long dry periods leave less water to move through soil and replenish underground stores. The response can be delayed, and falling groundwater may also reflect extra pumping rather than reduced replenishment alone.
urbanization->aquifer_recharge_failure: Paved surfaces and drains can send rainwater to rivers before it soaks underground. Local leaks, storage basins and designs that let water soak in can offset or reverse that effect.
deforestation->aquifer_recharge_failure: Removing forests changes roots, soil and water use. It can reduce groundwater replenishment where runoff increases, but can increase it where trees previously used much of the water. Local evidence is needed.
aquifer_recharge_failure->water_stress: Less water replenishing underground stores can reduce dependable supplies and increase saltwater intrusion near coasts. Large reserves or lower pumping can protect users from short-term shortages.
old_growth_forest_logging->forest_fragme: Logging and access roads can create gaps and edges in older forests. The amount of separation depends on how harvesting is done and must be assessed across the wider landscape.
old_growth_forest_logging->biodiversity_: Removing older trees can reduce nesting holes, dead wood and layered habitats used by specialised wildlife. Effects differ between forests, and some managed areas retain or regain important features.
old_growth_forest_logging->carbon_emissi: Logging moves carbon from living trees into wood products and material that may decay. The overall emissions depend on regrowth, product lifespan and the time assessed. Harvested wood is not automatically equal to carbon released.
temp->rainforest_savannization: Heat increases plants' demand for water and can add to stress from drought, fire and land use. It may favour a more open tropical landscape, but temperature alone does not determine the outcome and the thresholds remain uncertain.
drought_persistence->rainforest_savanniz: Repeated drought can kill trees, increase fire risk and favour plants adapted to drier conditions. A single drought does not prove a permanent change from forest to open vegetation.
rainforest_savannization->biodiversity_i: A lasting shift to more open vegetation removes conditions needed by many forest species. The new landscape may support other wildlife, so the loss concerns the original forest community rather than all biodiversity.
temp->pollen_allergen_spikes: Warmer seasons and later autumn frost can let some plants release pollen for longer. The cited monitoring covers a limited network and measures season length, not every person's exposure or the total pollen produced.
carbon_emission->pollen_allergen_spikes: Carbon dioxide building up in the air can increase pollen or allergen production in some plants. Responses vary by species and conditions. Nearby emissions do not directly establish nearby pollen levels.
pollen_allergen_spikes->air_pollution_he: Pollen can irritate the nose and eyes or worsen asthma in people who are sensitive to it. Outdoor counts do not measure each person's exposure, and many exposed people have no symptoms.
marine_heatwaves->fisheries_range_redist: Unusually hot seawater can move suitable habitat farther away, deeper or toward the poles. Some fish move, while others stay, adjust or return after the event.
oceanic_deoxygenation->fisheries_range_r: Less oxygen can reduce the depths and temperatures fish can tolerate and change where their food lives. Responses differ between species, and local oxygen loss may come from nutrient pollution as well as climate change.
ocean_acidification->fisheries_range_red: Changing seawater chemistry can affect growth, reproduction, prey and habitat. It may contribute to changes in where fish live, but direct evidence is generally weaker than for warming and numbers can change without movement.
fisheries_range_redistribution->fishery_: Fish moving across borders can change which fleets can reach them and challenge existing catch agreements. Shared surveys and flexible agreements can manage the change without conflict.
temp->desertification_frontiers: Warming can increase drying and erosion pressures on dryland soil and plants. It does not prove lasting land damage on its own. Rain, management and several measures of land condition need to be considered.
drought_persistence->desertification_fro: Repeated drought can reduce plant cover and leave soil exposed to erosion. Healthy or restored land may recover when rain returns, so a dry period is not automatically permanent degradation.
industry_farming->desertification_fronti: Poorly suited farming can remove protective plants, erode soil, drain water reserves or leave salts behind. Well-managed crops, irrigation and restoration can instead maintain or improve dryland condition.
desertification_frontiers->food_insecuri: Long-lasting damage to soil, vegetation and water supplies can make food production less reliable. Income, imports, technology and public support can protect households from some of the resulting losses.
pesticide_spray_drift_zones->air_polluti: Drifting farm chemicals can reach workers, homes and schools through air or direct contact. Harm depends on the chemical and dose. Detecting drift alone does not establish a health effect.
pesticide_spray_drift_zones->pollinator_: Chemicals drifting off a field can reach flowers, water or nesting sites used by pollinating insects. Detecting them does not prove declining pollination. Effects depend on the product, species, amount and timing.
desertification_frontiers->dust_storm_fr: Bare or damaged dryland can expose loose soil that strong winds lift into the air. Degraded land does not create a storm without suitable winds, and many dust sources are natural.
drought_persistence->dust_storm_frequenc: Drought can dry the surface and reduce plant cover, leaving more material available for wind to lift. Strong winds and loose sediment are still needed, and protective soil crusts can limit dust.
industry_farming->dust_storm_frequency: Disturbing dry soil and removing cover can make farmland more vulnerable to wind erosion. Keeping plants, windbreaks and suitable grazing or ploughing practices can instead reduce dust losses.
dust_storm_frequency->air_pollution_heal: Windblown mineral particles can worsen air quality near their source and far downwind. Health effects depend on the particles and actual exposure. A visible dust plume alone does not establish illness.
temp->atmospheric_river_intensification: Warmer air can carry more water vapour, allowing long bands of moist air to transport more water. This does not guarantee more events or stronger winds in every place, and historical trends depend on the available record.
atmospheric_river_intensification->extre: A strong, long-lasting stream of moist air can produce heavy rain or snow when mountains or fronts lift it. Without suitable lifting, direction or duration, it may mainly provide useful water rather than an extreme event.
atmospheric_river_intensification->river: Sustained rain from a band of moist air can sharply raise river flow, especially on wet ground or melting snow. Dry soil, reservoirs and shorter events can limit runoff and allow beneficial replenishment.
aviation_demand_growth->aviation_condens: More flights create more opportunities for exhaust to form ice clouds at cruising height. Persistent trails form only in suitable cold, humid air. Flight numbers alone cannot predict them.
aviation_condensation_trails->cloud_albe: Some aircraft trails spread into thin ice clouds, changing reflected sunlight and escaping heat. Most disappear quickly, and their warming and cooling effects can partly offset each other.
aviation_condensation_trails->solar_radi: Persistent aircraft ice clouds both reflect sunlight and trap outgoing heat. The assessed global net effect is warming, but uncertainty is large and individual trails can have little effect or cause cooling depending on place and time.
methane->methane_hydroxyl_sink_loss: Removing methane from air uses highly reactive chemicals called hydroxyl radicals. More methane can use some of that capacity and stay longer, but other chemical and weather changes can increase removal instead.
carbon_monoxide->methane_hydroxyl_sink_l: Carbon monoxide also reacts with hydroxyl radicals, which help remove methane. More carbon monoxide can leave less removal capacity, although other reactions can recycle these chemicals and change the result.
methane_hydroxyl_sink_loss->solar_radiat: If the air's chemical ability to remove methane weakens, methane can remain longer and trap more heat. Other removal processes can offset this, and the size of the effect is difficult to measure directly everywhere.
el_nino->walker_circulation_shift: Warmer central and eastern Pacific water shifts rising air and tropical storms eastward. This can weaken or move the usual east-to-west circulation, but one event does not establish a long-term trend.
la_nina->walker_circulation_shift: Cooler central and eastern Pacific water can strengthen the usual pattern of rising air in the west and sinking air in the east. The response differs between events and does not by itself explain a decades-long trend.
walker_circulation_shift->monsoon_volati: Changes in tropical rising and sinking air can shift where rain falls. Some monsoon regions respond, while local weather processes can outweigh the distant influence.
subsea_cables->subsea_cable_landing_chok: Several cables sharing a landing area, power supply or land connection may fail together. More cables provide protection only when these supporting routes and services are sufficiently independent.
compound_coastal_flooding->subsea_cable_: Coastal flooding can affect cable landing stations and their power or land connections. Shared locations increase the risk of several links failing together, while protection, backup power and separated routes can prevent disruption.
subsea_cable_landing_chokepoint->critica: Losing shared cable landing or power facilities can remove several communication paths at once. Essential services are less affected where traffic can switch to independent routes with enough spare capacity.
marine_fisheries_collapse->fishery_borde: Fewer accessible fish can increase competition over catches and income where access is contested. Scarcity does not inevitably cause conflict. Good agreements and recovery plans can reduce the pressure.
fishery_protein_dependence->fishery_bord: Communities heavily dependent on fish face higher costs when access is lost. This can make catch-sharing changes difficult, but dependence can also encourage cooperation rather than conflict.
fishery_border_dispute_zones->conflict_r: Repeated confrontations or failed fishing agreements can worsen political tensions. Most disputes remain within negotiation, and existing tensions may cause fishing incidents rather than result from them.
temp->convective_instability_shift: Warm, moist air near the ground can rise more strongly if the air above allows it. Warming higher up, dryness or a layer that blocks rising air can prevent this potential from becoming a storm.
convective_instability_shift->extreme_pr: More strongly rising air can support heavier rain, but moisture, storm movement and organisation also matter. High potential energy can remain unused, while very moist storms can produce extreme rain with little of it.
convective_instability_shift->lightning_: Strong rising air can move water and ice through clouds in ways that help generate lightning. Other cloud conditions matter, so one measure of atmospheric energy is not a lightning forecast.
temp->lightning_regime_shifts: Warming changes moisture, rising air and the ice processes involved in lightning. Models disagree on how these effects combine, so the direction of future lightning change remains uncertain in many regions.
lightning_regime_shifts->lightning_fire_: Lightning reaching the ground can ignite vegetation when it is dry enough and rain does not put the fire out. Most flashes do not start a recorded fire, and later spread depends on weather and response.
air_conditioning_refrigerants->cfc_satur: Older cooling equipment can leak CFCs or HCFCs that damage the ozone layer. This pathway excludes modern replacement gases that contain no ozone-damaging chlorine or bromine, and equipment counts alone do not measure leaks.
refrigerant_phase_down->cfc_saturated_la: Controls on old ozone-damaging gases reduce new supply, while recovery and destruction prevent releases from existing equipment. Improvement is slow because stored gases can still leak and some remain in the air for many decades.
cfc_saturated_layers->stratospheric_chlo: High in the atmosphere, sunlight breaks down certain gases and releases chemicals containing chlorine or bromine that destroy ozone. Cold polar clouds can speed the process, but gas levels alone do not predict each season's ozone loss.
refrigerant_phase_down->stratospheric_ch: Reducing ozone-damaging cooling gases lowers the future supply of reactive chlorine and bromine high in the atmosphere. Recovery is slow and uneven because old equipment, long gas lifetimes and weather still matter.
stratospheric_chlorine_sinks->stratosphe: Ozone absorbs energy and warms the upper atmosphere. Losing it can cool the affected layer, although carbon dioxide also causes cooling there and cold conditions can themselves encourage ozone loss.
dust_storm_frequency->snowpack_dust_soot: Dust storms can carry mineral particles to mountain snow, where they settle in layers. A storm elsewhere does not prove deposition at a particular site, and buried dust may not reach the surface until later melting.
desertification_frontiers->snowpack_dust: Damaged dryland can supply loose dust, but reaching snow also requires the right winds and route. Some dust sources are natural, so identifying the source needs evidence beyond nearby land damage.
snowpack_dust_soot_coverage->snowmelt_ti: Dark dust on snow absorbs sunlight and can bring earlier melting and runoff. Fresh snow can bury it and clouds reduce its effect, so the size of the timing change must be assessed locally.
snowpack_dust_soot_coverage->hydrologica: Faster snowmelt can send stored water into streams over a shorter spring period. Earlier melting does not always mean damaging floods: reservoirs can slow the flow, and total runoff may fall as exposed land loses more water to the air.
pesticide_spray_drift_zones->agrochemica: Drifting farm chemicals can settle directly on water or on surfaces that later drain into it. A drift event does not prove contamination at a particular site, and detected residues may have other sources.
agrochemical_water_sinks->freshwater_eco: Some farm chemicals can harm aquatic plants and animals when exposure is high enough or repeated. Detection alone does not prove harm, and crossing a screening threshold does not establish that a whole ecosystem has failed.
agrochemical_water_sinks->pesticide_bioa: Some chemicals in water bind to sediment and enter animals through water or food. Many break down quickly or do not build up appreciably, while older contaminated sediment can remain a source after water levels fall.
pesticide_bioaccumulation_chains->biodiv: Chemicals stored in animal tissues can affect survival, reproduction or development if the dose is harmful. Finding a residue alone does not prove population damage, and effects differ between chemicals and food webs.
forest_fragmentation->biodiversity_corri: Splitting forests into separate patches can make it harder for some species to move, breed or recolonise an area. Other species can cross the gaps, so a map alone does not prove that movement has stopped.
urbanization->biodiversity_corridors_dis: Development can remove habitat and add roads, noise or light that interfere with wildlife movement. Parks, gardens and safe crossings can preserve useful links for some species.
biodiversity_corridors_disruption->biodi: Less movement between habitats can isolate populations and limit access to food or cooler places. Connections are not always the main constraint, and they can also spread disease or invasive species.
temp->avian_migration_disruptions: Warmer seasons can change when food becomes available along bird migration routes. Some birds adjust successfully while others do not. An early arrival in one year does not prove a lasting mismatch.
biodiversity_corridors_disruption->avian: Losing resting or seasonal habitats can force migrating birds to travel farther or leave them with less food. Some use alternative sites, so fewer birds at one stop does not by itself prove a failing route.
avian_migration_disruptions->biodiversit: Repeated difficulty finding food or suitable habitat during migration can reduce survival and breeding success. A changed route or date can also be a useful adjustment, so population effects need evidence across the birds' full yearly cycle.
temp->high_altitude_forest_shrinkage: Warming can dry lower forest margins and prevent young trees from establishing, while allowing trees to grow higher where cold once limited them. Both boundaries and local moisture need to be checked before claiming the forest is shrinking overall.
drought_persistence->high_altitude_fores: Long dry periods can weaken mountain trees and prevent regrowth after damage. Some forests recover when moisture returns, so a short decline in greenness is not proof of permanent loss.
wildfire_regime_shift->high_altitude_for: Severe fires can remove mountain trees and seed sources. Lasting forest loss occurs when trees cannot regrow. Many forests normally recover from fire, and some lower-intensity fires support renewal.
high_altitude_forest_shrinkage->biodiver: Lasting changes in mountain forests alter shelter, food and connections used by wildlife. Some species lose habitat while others benefit from openings or forest expansion, so population changes need separate evidence.
temp->amphibian_chytrid_fungus_spreads: Temperature affects both amphibians and the fungus that infects their skin. Infection can be greatest at intermediate temperatures, so warming may increase suitability in cold places but reduce it in already hot places.
amphibian_chytrid_fungus_spreads->biodiv: Severe fungal infection can damage amphibian skin function and cause death. Many infections do not cause visible disease, and some populations recover despite continued exposure. Deaths need a confirmed cause.
invasive_species_encroachment->amphibian: Introduced animals carrying the fungus can expose native amphibians as they move between waters. Finding both together does not prove transmission. Timing, movement or genetic evidence is needed.
plastics_petrochemicals->aerosolized_mic: Wear, processing and weathering can release tiny plastic fibres or fragments that enter the air. Plastic use alone does not measure airborne releases, and suspected particles need chemical confirmation.
urbanization->aerosolized_microplastics: Dense urban activity creates opportunities for small plastic particles to enter or re-enter the air from wear, handling and dust. Cities also receive particles from elsewhere, so location alone does not identify the source.
road_freight_diesel_lock_in->aerosolized: Heavy road use wears tyres and can release tiny fragments containing synthetic materials. Not every dark roadside particle comes from tyres, and freight-specific claims need evidence about vehicle types.
amoc->gulf_stream_slowdown: Part of the strong northward Atlantic surface current belongs to the ocean's wider overturning circulation. Changes in that wider system can affect it, but winds also drive the current, so the two are not interchangeable.
north_atlantic_oscillation->gulf_stream_: Long-lasting North Atlantic pressure and wind changes can influence the position of the current farther downstream. Relationships vary by place and time, and matching patterns alone do not prove one direct cause.
gulf_stream_slowdown->coastal_inundation: A weaker current through the Florida Straits is associated with higher sea levels along nearby Atlantic coasts. Many other factors control flooding there, so a rising tide gauge alone does not identify a change in the current.
north_atlantic_oscillation->subpolar_gyr: North Atlantic pressure patterns change winds and heat exchange over the ocean. These can strengthen, weaken or shift its northern circular flow, but no atmospheric phase gives one fixed response everywhere.
ocean_salinity_stratification->subpolar_: Changes in salt content alter seawater density and can change northern Atlantic circulation. Fresher water does not automatically mean weaker flow because temperature, winds and the water carried by currents also matter.
temp->subpolar_gyre_weakening: Warmer or less strongly cooled surface water may sink less and change northern Atlantic flow. Temperature alone cannot determine the response because salt content and transported heat also affect density and circulation.
marine_fisheries_collapse->trophic_casca: Losing large numbers of harvested predators or other consumers can change the species they eat and those below them. A chain reaction needs evidence at several levels, not just one declining species.
invasive_species_encroachment->trophic_c: An introduced predator or competitor can change who eats what in a food web. These changes may spread through several connected groups of organisms.
coral_reef_fragmentation->trophic_cascad: Broken reef habitat can remove shelter and feeding areas. This changes how predators and prey encounter each other and may affect the wider food web.
trophic_cascade_collapses->marine_food_w: Persistent losses or imbalances between predators and prey can remove feeding relationships. The remaining community may have fewer species able to perform similar roles.
mining_critical_minerals->deep_sea_minin: Collecting material from the seabed and releasing processing water can stir up fine particles. These form cloudy plumes near the bottom or within the water above it.
deep_sea_mining_dust->biodiversity_intac: Particles from seabed mining can settle over habitats or interfere with feeding. Effects depend on the organisms and the area reached by the plume.
forest_fragmentation->genetic_diversity_: Splitting habitat into smaller pieces can leave fewer animals or plants breeding in each area. With less movement between groups, inherited variety may decline over generations.
biodiversity_corridors_disruption->genet: Losing usable routes between habitats can reduce breeding between separated groups. Small, isolated populations can then lose genetic variety more easily.
wildlife_habitat_patches->genetic_divers: Small or shrinking habitat patches may support fewer breeding individuals. Genetic variety can fall if too few newcomers join the population.
genetic_diversity_bottlenecks->biodivers: Less inherited variety and more breeding between close relatives can reduce a population's ability to adjust to change. Some affected populations may become less likely to persist.
nutrient_pollution->jellyfish_swarm_surg: Nutrient-rich coastal water can increase food for some jellyfish and create conditions they tolerate well. The response depends on the species and local water conditions.
coastal_hypoxia->jellyfish_swarm_surges: Some jellyfish tolerate low oxygen better than fish and other competitors. Oxygen-poor conditions may therefore shift the balance in their favour.
urbanization->jellyfish_swarm_surges: Piers, seawalls and other underwater structures can provide places for the attached life stage of some jellyfish. More suitable surfaces can support later releases of free-swimming animals.
jellyfish_swarm_surges->fish_landing_sup: Dense jellyfish groups can clog fishing nets, harm catches or affect fish-farm enclosures. Local fishing operations may be interrupted while the event lasts.
drought_persistence->savannah_tree_cover: Repeated dry periods can make it harder for savanna trees to establish and survive. Effects are greater where rain and soil already limit growth.
wildfire_regime_shift->savannah_tree_cov: Frequent or severe fire can kill young woody plants before they grow large enough to withstand burning. This can reduce tree cover over time.
industry_farming->savannah_tree_cover_de: Clearing land for crops or heavy livestock pressure can reduce trees in savannas. The link applies where those activities overlap the vegetation being measured.
savannah_tree_cover_decline->biodiversit: Lasting loss of savanna trees removes shade, food, nesting sites and shelter. Species that depend on that woody layer may decline.
mining_critical_minerals->heavy_metal_bi: Mining and processing can release metals from waste, drainage and disturbed material. Some can enter water, food and animal tissues.
acid_rain_deposition->heavy_metal_bioacc: More acidic conditions can make some metals easier to dissolve and move. Exposure may increase where those metals are already present in soil or water.
deep_sea_mining_dust->heavy_metal_bioacc: Mining plumes can carry metal-containing particles or dissolved metals to deep-water organisms. This creates a possible exposure route near the affected area.
heavy_metal_bioaccumulation->biodiversit: Enough metal building up in tissues can harm survival, reproduction or behaviour. Effects depend on the metal, dose and species exposed.
extreme_precipitation_intensity->riparia: Heavy rain and flood peaks can increase water force against river banks. Saturated or undercut banks may collapse where they are vulnerable.
hydrological_runoff_surges->riparian_zon: A rapid rise in runoff can increase river depth and speed. Banks erode when the force of moving water exceeds the ground's resistance.
watershed_forest_loss->riparian_zone_ero: Losing trees can increase runoff and sediment reaching rivers. Where bank vegetation is also lost, fewer roots hold the bank in place.
riparian_zone_erosion->freshwater_ecosys: Continued river-bank loss can add fine sediment, bury habitat and remove shade. River plants and animals may lose suitable places to live.
drought_persistence->overstory_tree_mort: Long water shortages can disrupt a tree's water transport and weaken its defences. The air's demand for moisture also matters, so temperature alone is not enough to describe the exposure.
wildfire_regime_shift->overstory_tree_mo: Severe fires can kill tall canopy trees by burning crowns or damaging bark and roots. Some injured trees die later, including after insect attack.
bark_beetle_epidemics->overstory_tree_mo: Large bark-beetle populations can attack and kill host trees. The trees selected are not always simply the ones that were already most stressed.
overstory_tree_mortality->forest_dieback: When many dominant trees die across adjoining areas, the losses form a wider episode of forest die-off. Mapping the pattern helps distinguish it from isolated tree deaths.
nutrient_pollution->freshwater_mussel_de: Excess nutrients can change oxygen, algae and ammonia levels in freshwater. Sensitive young mussels may be harmed where exposure becomes high enough.
riverine_habitat_fragmentation->freshwat: Dams and other barriers can change flow and prevent movement of fish that carry young mussels during part of their life cycle. This can limit mussel spread and recovery.
drought_persistence->freshwater_mussel_d: Long periods of low water can expose mussel beds, increase heat and concentrate pollution. Fish needed for the mussels' life cycle may also lose access.
freshwater_mussel_depletion->freshwater_: Large, lasting mussel losses remove animals that filter water and help stabilise riverbeds. Nutrient movement and habitats supported by dense mussel groups may also change.
carbon_emission->solar_radiation_trappin: Carbon dioxide accumulating in the air reduces the heat Earth can release to space. Yearly emissions alone do not determine the change because oceans and land absorb a varying share. The assessment uses global concentration relative to a stated baseline.
methane->solar_radiation_trapping: More methane across the atmosphere traps additional heat and also affects ozone and water vapour high above Earth. A local leak or brief concentration spike is not equivalent to a change in the global annual heat balance.
nitrous_oxide->solar_radiation_trapping: Nitrous oxide lasts long enough to spread through the atmosphere and add to heat trapping. Its effect is assessed from global abundance with other gases accounted for, so a sector's emissions cannot directly replace that measurement.
solar_radiation_trapping->temp: When more energy stays in Earth's climate system than leaves it, the land and oceans warm as the system adjusts. Short-term regional temperatures can still move in the opposite direction, and the energy measure is not a temperature observation.
temp->bark_beetle_epidemics: Warmer seasons can let some bark beetles develop faster and survive winter in greater numbers. Excessive heat or a lack of suitable trees can instead limit outbreaks.
drought_persistence->bark_beetle_epidemi: Severe drought can weaken a tree's protective sap and other defences against beetles. The response varies: moderate dryness can hinder some beetles, and drought links are weak for some species.
wildfire_regime_shift->bark_beetle_epide: Trees injured but not killed by fire may become suitable hosts for some beetles. Fire can also kill the insects or their hosts, so a burned area does not automatically predict an outbreak.
bark_beetle_epidemics->forest_dieback_ar: Large beetle populations can overwhelm susceptible trees and disrupt their water and nutrient supply. Wide areas may die, but other stresses often contribute and delayed surveys can make the cause difficult to separate.
deforestation->zoonotic_disease_outbreak: Forest clearing changes contact between wildlife, domestic animals and people. This can create opportunities for germs to cross species, but most clearing does not cause an outbreak and the transmission route needs evidence.
industry_farming->zoonotic_disease_outbr: Crowded animals, frequent movement and poor disease controls can help germs persist or reach workers and food. Effective controls can reduce some risks, and outcomes differ by germ and farming system.
urbanization->zoonotic_disease_outbreaks: Urban growth can change contact with animals through habitat expansion, waste and food systems. It does not identify an outbreak's source by itself, and better services can reduce risk.
zoonotic_disease_outbreaks->humanitarian: An expanding animal-to-human disease outbreak can increase needs for testing, care and containment at the same time. A resource gap occurs only if these needs exceed available response capacity.
industry_farming->methane: Livestock, manure and flooded rice fields can release methane, with amounts depending on farming methods. Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change reports global farm-gate methane emissions of 142 million tonnes per year, plus or minus 42 million, during 2007–2016. This excludes later food-processing and delivery stages.
industry_farming->carbon_emission: Farming can release carbon dioxide through land conversion, energy use and the production of inputs. The amount depends on which activities, gases and stages the source includes. Methane and nitrous oxide need separate accounting.
industry_farming->biodiversity_intactnes: Simpler habitats, pesticide exposure, nutrient losses and land clearing can harm plants and animals around farms. The effect depends on local practices and documented exposure.
industry_farming->coastal_hypoxia: Nutrients lost from farms can reach coastal water and encourage growth that later uses up oxygen. The connection depends on transport downstream and the actual oxygen response.
industry_farming->anoxic_dead_zones: Farm nutrients can contribute to coastal areas with very little oxygen after extra algae decay. Evidence is needed that the nutrients reached the water and helped cause the oxygen loss.
industry_farming->pollinator_service_dec: Large areas of one crop, fewer habitats and pesticide exposure can reduce food and safety for pollinating insects. Farm management and the surrounding landscape affect the outcome.
industry_farming->food_insecurity: Farms dependent on costly inputs or facing damaged soil and limited water can become less reliable. Food access is affected when these pressures change harvests, prices or household income.
industry_farming->soil_microbial_depleti: Frequent soil disturbance, few crop types and chemical pressures can change the communities living in farm soil. Local measurements are needed to show which organisms and functions are affected.
industry_farming->air_pollution_health_b: Agricultural burning, ammonia and other farm emissions can contribute to air pollution. Health impacts depend on the pollutants released and people's actual exposure.
deforestation->carbon_emission: Clearing forests can release stored carbon and reduce later uptake by trees. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change land assessment reports a broad literature range of 0.5–3.5 billion tonnes of carbon per year from tropical forest loss and damage (reported as the weight of carbon alone).
deforestation->water_stress: Losing forests changes how water enters soil, returns to the air and reaches rivers. This can worsen shortages where those forest functions help maintain dependable supplies, but the response is local.
deforestation->floodplain_exposure: Forest loss can increase sediment and rapid runoff reaching rivers. Flood risk depends on how the water moves downstream and whether people or buildings are exposed.
deforestation->biodiversity_intactness_l: Clearing and splitting forests removes habitats used by native species. Some plants and animals may become less common or disappear from the affected landscape.
deforestation->wildfire_regime_shift: Damaged or cleared forests can interact with drying and human ignitions to change fire patterns. The result also depends on available vegetation and land management.
deforestation->topsoil_erosion_accelerat: Removing trees leaves soil with less protection from rain and fewer roots holding it. Erosion can increase on vulnerable slopes during heavy rain.
deforestation->freshwater_ecosystem_coll: Forest loss can change river flows, water quality and stream habitats. Freshwater wildlife may be harmed where these catchment changes reach the water.
deforestation->migration: Losing forest-based jobs, food or other benefits can add pressure for people to move. Economic, political and climate conditions also shape that decision.
ice_sheet_mass_loss->sea_level_rise: Ice lost from land adds water to the ocean and raises average sea level. Greenland's measured loss during 1992–2020 was equivalent to 13.5 millimetres globally, with an assessed range of 11.4–15.6 millimetres.
